Vienna
THE MONTE CRISTO STRINGS
Vienna, capital of Mitteleuropa on the shores of the Blue Danube, is once again "the
musician's holy city". The new State Opera serves as the scene for many a dazzling reception,
reminiscent of that carefree era of wine-women-and-waltz-time.
The Viennese flock to hear the Vienna Philharmonic, the Vienna Symphony and the
Volksoper, where the "Merry Widow", symbol of "Vienna" throughout the world for a
generation, is still the all-time favorite. The silvery voices of the Vienna Boys' Choir still fill the
Hofburg Chapel, and even the famous white Lippizaner horses at the Spanish Riding School
perform their graceful pirouettes to the strains of Mozart and Strauss. Viennese strolling
beneath the baroque arcades hum the lilting "Emperor Waltz"; the bittersweet sound of the
zither floats up from the smoky kellers; and Schrammel quartets in the taverns sentimentalize
on the new wine and lilac time.
Music is the life of Vienna, and what other nations say with words, the Viennese say with
music. The Viennese air has inspired composers such as Beethoven, Bach, Brahms, Schubert,
Bruckner, Mahler, Gluck, Strauss and Lehar, to name but a few.
Rivaling Vienna's status as the music capital of Europe is its prestige as an art center. Few
museums in the world are so richly endowed not only with masterpieces by Brueghel,
Rembrandt, Titian, Raphael and Rubens but also with antiquities from Egypt, Rome
and Greece.
Like a woman "entre deux ages" who dislikes brilliant lights and feels happier in the dim of
twilight, Vienna is at its best i: the evening, when a misty, timeless beauty envelopes the old
squares with their baroque palaces, many of them still occupied. Hofburg Palace with its
ornate imperial apartments remains a showplace for the priceless treasures of the Hapsburgs
as does Schonbrunn Palace. State receptions, staged in many of these royal settings, recall
Franz Josef and the splendor of the Empire. Beneath the crystal chandeliers, the champagne
flows and hearts beat in three-quarter time; heels click, hands are kissed and flirtations
flourish: then, Vienna becomes a city of gay abandon, senuous and seductive, waltzing the
night away.
The Viennese are a hospitable, gracious people who typify that indefinable word, "gemutlich"
They like their coffee with globs of whipped cream, and favor such dishes as wiener schnitzel
and golden goulash. Some say they are as proud of their strudel as they are of their Strauss.
The ideal vantage point for an eye-astonishing glimpse of the city is the top of St. Stephen's
Cathedral alte Steffi" as the Viennese affectionately call this beloved landmark, dating
from 1147. Another high point is the huge ("Third Man") ferris wheel in the Prater, an
amusement park on the Danube Canal.
Nothing, however, brings to mind the gaiety and beauty of Vienna as does the waltz, the
melodies of Lehar and Strauss which set the world a-whirling a century ago. As performed
by the Monte Cristo strings, this repertoire of old favorites captures the passionate heartbeat
of Vienna itself.
